title: Can Deterministic Network Verification Reduce Undetected Faults in LLM‑Generated Configurations?
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study to test whether interposing a deterministic network verifier reduces the proportion of LLM‑generated network configurations that would execute with operational faults in an isolated emulation environment. Under a shared_initial_candidate design (one identical initial LLM candidate per intent evaluated both without and with verification), we evaluated 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) in an emulator. Primary result: baseline and guarded evaluations both produced valid, non‑faulting emulator executions for all 72 pairs (n_11 = 72), yielding a paired difference of 0.0 (95% bootstrap CI 0.0–0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). Confirmatory interpretation: for the chosen model, task set, and shared_initial_candidate semantics, the verifier did not reduce undetected faults because none occurred in the baseline (ceiling effect). We describe the preregistered design, deterministic execution manifest, exact analysis outcomes, and limitations; and we emphasise that alternate designs (independent per‑condition generations, adversarial/fault‑injection tasks, multi‑model sampling) are needed to measure verifier utility in less constrained settings.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device‑level network configurations. Past work reports encouraging task‑level translation accuracy but warns of operational risks from semantic errors, incorrect ordering, and protocol misuse that can cause policy violations, outages, or security regressions [1], [2]. A commonly proposed mitigation is a generate–verify–repair (GVR) architecture that interposes deterministic validators (e.g., header‑space/forwarding/policy checkers) before applying changes to live infrastructure [3], [4]. We preregistered a focused, paired experiment to answer the question: does coupling an LLM generator with a canonical deterministic network verifier materially reduce the fraction of LLM candidates that would execute with operational faults, compared with executing the same LLM candidate without verification? Crucially, the preregistered design uses shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial LLM generation is produced per intent and that exact candidate is evaluated under both conditions. This design isolates verifier detection of faults in the identical candidate rather than differences arising from independent generation or prompt engineering.
sections.related_work: Several recent studies demonstrate intent→configuration translation using LLMs in constrained settings and vendor dialects, showing promising accuracy on curated tasks but noting safety gaps for live execution [1]. Multi‑agent and tool‑augmented NetOps prototypes integrate validators and tooling to reduce regressions, but public, systematic evidence of verifier utility on end‑to‑end execution outcomes is limited [2]. Generate–verify–repair patterns and deterministic‑oracle repair loops have been proposed and empirically instantiated in code and software‑engineering domains to reconcile stochastic generation with deterministic checks [3]. Classical static network verifiers (header‑space/NetPlumber/Batfish family) provide fast forwarding and policy checks and are natural verifier candidates for NetOps GVR stacks [4]. Our study addresses the empirical gap by executing a preregistered, paired test that couples an LLM generator with a deterministic network verifier and measures emulator execution outcomes.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 preregistered the primary estimand as the paired reduction in the proportion of undetected operational faults (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Design and sampling: confirmatory paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics; 72 paired intents stratified across three topology complexity strata (preregistered). Generation and model: all initial generations used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version). Per the recorded execution configuration, sampling/runtime generation parameters were not set in the run artifacts (model_configuration.json records temperature = null and related sampling fields unset); null indicates no explicit sampling parameter was specified by the experimenter and the hosted provider default was used. This does not imply deterministic (temperature=0) sampling; exact provider default semantics and the full recorded model_configuration artifact are archived in the execution manifest. Adapter and verifier: the orchestration adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) produced one shared initial generation per intent; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed syntactic/semantic intent‑constraint checks and violation flagging. Execution contract and emulator: baseline = execute the shared LLM candidate in isolated emulator; guarded = run the deterministic verifier on the same shared candidate and, if the verifier flagged violations, treat the guarded outcome as prevented (no undetected executed fault); if not flagged, execute in emulator and record outcome. Retries and missingness: one initial generation per intent with preregistered transient‑error retries; excluded pairs and sensitivity analyses were prespecified. Analysis: the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor applied an exact paired binary test (McNemar‑style where appropriate), and bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, recorded seed) for descriptive rates. All design choices, exclusion rules, manifests, and raw outputs are archived in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Execution accounting: the registered run completed (execution_manifest). Planned_episode_count = 144; completed_episode_count = 144; model_calls_used = 72; complete_pair_count = 72. Observed contingency: every paired intent produced a valid, non‑faulting emulator execution in both baseline and guarded conditions. Contingency table counts: n_11 = 72, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI (percentile, 10,000 resamples; seed archived) = [0.0, 0.0]; the CI is degenerate because there was no observed variation across pairs (all outcomes identical). Secondary results: verifier true‑positive and false‑negative rates cannot be estimated here because no baseline emulator failures occurred; no verifier flags led to emulator‑observed faults. Missingness and exclusions: none; all preregistered pairs completed. Representative validator traces and scoring examples are archived in the evidence bundle.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and validity: the preregistered hypotheses required baseline faults for a verifier to demonstrate paired reduction. The observed ceiling (zero baseline faults) entails a null/degenerate confirmatory outcome: H1 is not supported because there were no undetected faults to reduce. This is a valid, evidence‑grounded scientific result for the chosen model, task corpus, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. It does not imply that verifiers are never useful; instead it shows verifier marginal utility depends on generator error rates, task realism, adversarial conditions, and sampling variability. Methodological implications: (1) shared_initial_candidate designs precisely measure verifier effect on the same candidate but cannot capture benefits that arise from using the verifier to trigger repairs or alternative generation strategies unless those repair calls are explicitly permitted and executed; (2) independent per‑condition generation or multi‑sample designs are needed to measure verifier utility under sampling variability; (3) adversarial/fault‑injection test sets increase the chance of generator faults and therefore the power to detect verifier benefits. Threats to validity: single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini); synthetic/emulated tasks differ from production environments; sampling parameters were unset in the recorded configuration (temperature=null) and provider defaults were used—this residual uncertainty is acknowledged. Future work should evaluate adversarial tasks, independent generation arms, additional models, and live‑device constraints to estimate verifier value under realistic error regimes.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, paired evaluation under shared_initial_candidate semantics to test whether a deterministic network verifier reduces undetected operational faults for LLM‑generated configurations. For the 72 preregistered intent pairs using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in an isolated emulator, baseline generations produced zero emulator faults and the verifier therefore did not change the outcome (paired difference 0.0, p = 1.0). The result highlights that verifier benefit is conditional on generator error prevalence and task realism; rigorous evaluation of GVR in NetOps requires adversarial, diverse, or independent‑generation designs to avoid ceiling effects. We release the execution manifest, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts to support follow‑on studies and community benchmarks.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock. Human role: a Research Director selected the topic family and approved the initial master prompt before autonomy. No human manually edited technical manuscript content after the lock. Models and core tools: initial generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version), orchestrated via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served as the verifier; isolated emulator images executed candidate configurations. Preregistration: study c1-gnr-vv-2026-0001 was frozen before observing outcomes. Immutable master prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts, verifier traces, and analysis code are archived in the registered execution manifest; the manifest and raw artifacts contain the full recorded model configuration (including that sampling fields were left unset) and the deterministic analysis logs.
limitations: Confirmatory ceiling/null outcome: the baseline generator produced zero emulator faults on the preregistered task set, preventing direct measurement of verifier detection benefit.
Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design measures verifier effect on the same generated candidate only and does not assess independent per‑condition generation or prompt‑sensitivity.
Single‑model scope: experiments used one declared model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across models or versions.
Synthetic/emulated tasks: task corpus and emulator executions differ from production devices and live traffic; external validity to production deployments is limited.

Sampling‑parameter uncertainty: the recorded model_configuration.json shows temperature = null (sampling parameters unset); null does not equal deterministic sampling (temperature=0) and provider defaults were applied—this residual uncertainty is acknowledged.

Residual contamination risk: deterministic provenance and exact‑match checks were applied, but private training‑data contamination of the hosted model cannot be fully ruled out and remains residual uncertainty.
